title: Needs vs Wants
concept: Needs are essential for health, safety, education, and daily living, while wants are optional purchases that make life more enjoyable.
learningObjective: Distinguish essential expenses from optional purchases and understand why needs usually come first.
primaryMisconception: Every item a person strongly desires is a need.
secondaryMisconceptions: Wants are always bad or wasteful.
An expensive item must be more important than a cheaper one.
keyTakeaway: Needs usually come first, but wants are not automatically bad.

screens.title: Too Much for One Wallet
screens.content: You have Rs. 5,000, but your list costs more. Which items should come first—and which can wait?
screens.illustration: A child holds Rs. 5,000 beside a list showing medicine, a school van, premium shoes, snacks, and a game controller.

screens.title: The Five-Item List
screens.content: Your family gives you Rs. 5,000 to cover several things this week. Your list includes medicine, school transport, premium shoes, snacks, and a game subscription.
screens.illustration: Five item cards appear beside a wallet marked Rs. 5,000.

screens.title: Something Must Wait
screens.content: The money will not cover everything. Choosing the shoes first could leave no money for medicine or your ride to school.
screens.illustration: The premium shoes move toward the wallet while the medicine and school van cards fade slightly.

screens.title: Fun Is Not Forbidden
screens.content: You do not have to remove every fun item forever. First, decide which items protect health, safety, education, or daily living.
screens.illustration: Two empty baskets labelled Need and Want appear, with the five item cards waiting to be sorted.

screens.title: What Should Guide You?
screens.question: Which plan should guide your first choices?

options.text: Cover medicine and school transport first
options.response: Good thinking. In this situation, those items support health and education.

options.text: Buy the most expensive item first
options.response: Price does not tell you how essential an item is.
Strong feelings can make something seem urgent, but they do not automatically make it essential.

options.text: Split the money equally across everything
options.response: An equal split may still leave important needs uncovered.

screens.title: Sort the Spending List
screens.instruction: Place each item under Need or Want for this situation.

scenarioAssumptions: The medicine is required for the person's health.
School transport is the available way to attend school.
The child already has safe, usable everyday shoes and food at home.

categories.label: Need
categories.description: Essential for health, safety, education, or daily living.

categories.label: Want
categories.description: Optional in this situation and can wait.

sortableItems.label: Medicine
sortableItems.explanation: The medicine is required for health in this story.

sortableItems.label: School transport
sortableItems.explanation: The transport allows the child to attend school in this story.

sortableItems.label: Premium shoes
sortableItems.explanation: The child already has safe, usable shoes, so the premium pair is optional.

sortableItems.label: Snacks
sortableItems.explanation: These extra snacks are optional because regular food is already available.

sortableItems.label: Game subscription
sortableItems.explanation: The subscription provides entertainment but is not essential for daily living.

placementRules: Each item must be placed in exactly one category.
Use the stated scenario assumptions when deciding.
There is one intended arrangement for this simplified story.

contextDependentItems.explanation: Basic shoes may be a need if a child has no safe pair. A premium upgrade can be a want.
Nutritious food is a need. Extra treats or snacks may be wants when regular food is available.
Transport may be a need when it is necessary for school, safety, or essential daily activities.

config.ambiguityExplanation: Needs and wants can change with the situation. This activity uses the details provided, not a rule that applies to every person.
config.validationMethod: Check every item after submission. Mark each placement as correct or needs another look.
config.retryBehavior: Keep correctly sorted items in place, return misplaced items to the centre, show their short explanation, and allow unlimited retries.

accessibilityAlternative.method: Let the learner select an item and choose Need or Want using buttons or a dropdown.
accessibilityAlternative.screenReaderInstruction: Select an item, choose Need or Want, and submit after all five items have a category.

feedback.success: Well sorted. You protected health and education first while recognising that fun choices can still matter later.
feedback.incorrect: A few items need another look. Ask whether each one is essential in this situation or can safely wait.
feedback.incomplete: Sort all five items before checking your answer.

screens.title: Important First, Enjoyable Later
screens.content: You sorted medicine and school transport as needs because, in this story, they support health and education. Premium shoes, snacks, and a game subscription are wants because they can be delayed without stopping essential daily activities. A need is something essential for health, safety, education, or daily living. A want is optional and adds enjoyment. Wants are not bad. The useful habit is to cover important needs first, then choose wants with the money left.
screens.simpleSummary: Cover important needs first, then choose wants with what remains.
screens.illustration: Medicine and school transport sit safely in a First basket. The three want items wait beside a saving jar.

screens.title: Birthday-Money Choice
screens.content: Hassan has Rs. 1,000 of birthday money. He needs a notebook for school and wants a toy car. He buys the notebook first, then saves the remaining money toward the toy. The toy is not bad; it simply comes after the school need.
screens.illustration: Hassan places a notebook in his school bag and drops the remaining money into a toy-car saving jar.

questions.text: Sana's school shoes no longer fit. She also wants a second toy. Which should usually come first?

options.feedback: Correct. Shoes that fit are needed for safety and school.
A toy can be enjoyable, but safe shoes are more essential in this situation.
A higher price does not automatically make an item more important.

questions.correctExplanation: Sana needs safe shoes that fit for school and daily use. A second toy is optional and can wait.
questions.misconceptionTested: An expensive item must be more important than a cheaper one.

questions.text: Bilal really wants a game pass and thinks about it all day. Does that make it a need?

options.text: No, wanting it strongly does not make it essential
options.feedback: Correct. A strong desire can still be a want.

options.text: Yes, because he wants it badly
options.feedback: Wanting something strongly does not make it essential for health, safety, education, or daily living.
Price does not decide whether something is a need.

questions.correctExplanation: The game pass may be enjoyable, but it remains optional. Feelings can be strong without changing a want into a need.
questions.misconceptionTested: Every item a person strongly desires is a need.

questions.text: You forgot your lunch and have enough pocket money for either lunch or decorative stickers. What should usually come first?

options.feedback: Correct. Food for the school day is the immediate need in this situation.
The stickers can be fun, but they can wait until the immediate food need is covered.
Wants are not bad. The goal is to cover the need first, then choose wants when possible.

questions.correctExplanation: Lunch supports health during the school day, while decorative stickers are optional. The stickers can be considered after the need is covered.
questions.misconceptionTested: Wants are always bad or wasteful.

screens.headline: Smart Sorter!
screens.message: You learned to put essential items first without treating every enjoyable choice as bad.
screens.progressMessage: Mission 2 complete in Become Money Smart.

screens.title: Home Item Detective
screens.instruction: Find one need and one want at home. Explain to someone why each item belongs in that group today.

reviewChecklist.notes: The mission focuses on distinguishing needs from wants and deciding which usually comes first.
It explains that needs and wants depend on context and that price or desire alone does not determine importance.
The mission uses school, shoes, snacks, games, pocket money, and clear consequences.
The mission does not discuss investing.
The mission does not discuss financial returns.
The mission does not discuss stocks or market prices.
Wants are presented as valid sources of enjoyment, and incorrect answers receive supportive feedback.
Scenario assumptions and context-dependent examples explain why the same item can be a need or want in different situations.
The mission uses Pakistani rupees, school transport, medicine, snacks, shoes, and familiar family decisions.
The learner sorts each expense by whether it is essential or optional under stated conditions.
The questions address strong desire, price, priority, and the belief that wants are bad.

reviewChecklist.item: Mission can be completed in under five minutes
reviewChecklist.notes: The mission is designed for approximately four minutes with one five-item sort and three short quiz questions.

reviewChecklist.item: Language matches the target reading level
reviewChecklist.notes: The wording is concrete, supportive, and suitable for children aged 8–12.
